blocks.body:
Two tanks of brine are connected by pipes; salt flows from each into the other at a rate proportional to the amount present. Two masses on a line are joined by springs; each one's acceleration depends on where both are. In both cases there are several unknown functions, and the derivative of each depends on all of them. A single equation like $y' = ky$ is no longer enough: we need a system.

The good news is that linear systems have a complete theory, and it is the theory of [[eigen|eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] in disguise. The aim of this page is to find all solutions of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ for a constant matrix $A$, to understand the three cases (real, complex and repeated eigenvalues), and to handle a forcing term.

blocks.title: From equations to a matrix
blocks.body:
A first-order linear system in $n$ unknowns $x_1(t), \dots, x_n(t)$ is

$$\mathbf x'(t) = A(t)\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf g(t),$$

where $\mathbf x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^T$, $A(t)$ is an $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf g(t)$ a vector. It is homogeneous if $\mathbf g = 0$. On this page $A$ is usually constant.

Any linear equation of order $n$ turns into such a system (see [[ode-linear]]). For $y'' + py' + qy = 0$ set $x_1 = y$ and $x_2 = y'$; then $x_1' = x_2$ and $x_2' = -qx_1 - px_2$, so

$$\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2\end{pmatrix}' = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -q & -p\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2\end{pmatrix}.$$

Conversely, systems arise directly. Masses $m = 1$ at positions $x_1, x_2$ (measured from rest), joined to two walls and to each other by three identical springs of stiffness 1, satisfy $x_1'' = -2x_1 + x_2$ and $x_2'' = x_1 - 2x_2$.

blocks.title: Basic theory
blocks.body:
Let $A(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ be continuous on an interval $I$, $t_0 \in I$ and $\mathbf x_0 \in \mathbb R^n$. Then:

1. The problem $\mathbf x' = A(t)\mathbf x + \mathbf g(t)$, $\mathbf x(t_0) = \mathbf x_0$ has exactly one solution, and it exists on all of $I$.
2. The solutions of the homogeneous system form a vector space of dimension $n$.
3. If $\mathbf x^{(1)}, \dots, \mathbf x^{(n)}$ are solutions of the homogeneous system and $W(t) = \det\bigl[\mathbf x^{(1)}(t) \cdots \mathbf x^{(n)}(t)\bigr]$ is their Wronskian, then $W(t) = W(t_0)\exp\int_{t_0}^t \operatorname{tr}A(s)\,ds$ (Abel–Liouville). In particular $W$ is either never zero (the solutions form a basis, called a fundamental set) or identically zero.

blocks.title: Proof of 2, assuming 1
blocks.body: Sums and scalar multiples of solutions of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ are solutions, because differentiation and multiplication by $A$ are linear; so the solutions form a vector space $S$. Define $E : S \to \mathbb R^n$ by $E(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x(t_0)$. This map is linear. It is onto, because by part 1 every initial vector $\mathbf x_0$ is the value at $t_0$ of some solution. It is one-to-one, because if $\mathbf x(t_0) = 0$ then $\mathbf x$ and the zero function solve the same initial value problem, so by uniqueness $\mathbf x = 0$. Hence $E$ is an isomorphism and $\dim S = n$ (see [[basis-dimension]]). The same argument shows that solutions are independent as functions exactly when their values at a single time are independent vectors, which is why $W(t_0) \ne 0$ at one point already forces $W \ne 0$ everywhere.

blocks.title: The eigenvalue method
blocks.body:
Try $\mathbf x(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ with a constant vector $\mathbf v \ne 0$. Then $\mathbf x' = \lambda e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ and $A\mathbf x = e^{\lambda t}A\mathbf v$, so this is a solution exactly when $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$. Each eigenvector gives a solution that moves along a fixed line through the origin, growing if $\lambda > 0$ and decaying if $\lambda < 0$.

If $A$ has $n$ independent eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_n$ (for instance if its eigenvalues are distinct), these $n$ solutions have Wronskian $\det[\mathbf v_1\cdots\mathbf v_n] \ne 0$ at $t = 0$, so by the theorem the general solution is

$$\mathbf x(t) = c_1e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_ne^{\lambda_nt}\mathbf v_n.$$

Another way to see this is to change variables. Writing $A = PDP^{-1}$ (see [[diagonalization]]) and $\mathbf y = P^{-1}\mathbf x$, the system becomes $\mathbf y' = D\mathbf y$, which is $n$ separate equations $y_i' = \lambda_iy_i$. Eigenvector coordinates decouple the system.

Complex eigenvalues. If $A$ is real and $\lambda = \alpha + i\beta$ with $\beta \ne 0$ has eigenvector $\mathbf v = \mathbf a + i\mathbf b$, then $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ is a complex solution, and since $A$ is real, its real and imaginary parts are separately real solutions:

$$e^{\alpha t}(\mathbf a\cos\beta t - \mathbf b\sin\beta t), \qquad e^{\alpha t}(\mathbf a\sin\beta t + \mathbf b\cos\beta t).$$

They rotate with angular frequency $\beta$ while growing or shrinking like $e^{\alpha t}$. The conjugate eigenvalue gives nothing new.

Repeated eigenvalues. If $\lambda$ is a double root of the characteristic polynomial but has only one independent eigenvector $\mathbf v$, a second solution is $e^{\lambda t}(t\mathbf v + \mathbf w)$, where $\mathbf w$ solves $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf w = \mathbf v$ (a generalised eigenvector; compare [[jordan]]). Substituting confirms it: the derivative is $e^{\lambda t}(\lambda t\mathbf v + \lambda\mathbf w + \mathbf v)$ and $A$ applied to $t\mathbf v + \mathbf w$ gives $\lambda t\mathbf v + \lambda\mathbf w + \mathbf v$.

blocks.title: Matrix exponential and fundamental matrix
blocks.body:
For a square matrix $A$,

$$e^{At} = I + tA + \frac{t^2A^2}{2!} + \frac{t^3A^3}{3!} + \cdots.$$

The series converges for every $t$, can be differentiated term by term to give $\frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = Ae^{At}$, and equals $I$ at $t = 0$. So $\mathbf x(t) = e^{At}\mathbf x_0$ is the solution with $\mathbf x(0) = \mathbf x_0$. More generally, any matrix $\Phi(t)$ whose columns form a fundamental set is a fundamental matrix, and $e^{At} = \Phi(t)\Phi(0)^{-1}$.

In practice: if $A = PDP^{-1}$ then $e^{At} = Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}$ with $e^{Dt} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{\lambda_it})$; if $A = \lambda I + N$ with $N^2 = 0$, then $e^{At} = e^{\lambda t}(I + tN)$, because $\lambda I$ commutes with $N$ and the series for $e^{Nt}$ stops after two terms.

blocks.title: Forcing terms
blocks.body:
For $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x + \mathbf g(t)$ the general solution is a particular solution plus the general homogeneous solution, exactly as for a single equation. If $\mathbf g = \mathbf b$ is constant and $A$ is invertible, the constant $\mathbf x^* = -A^{-1}\mathbf b$ is a particular solution (an equilibrium), and $\mathbf x - \mathbf x^*$ solves the homogeneous system.

In general, variation of parameters gives a formula. Look for $\mathbf x = e^{At}\mathbf c(t)$. Then $\mathbf x' = Ae^{At}\mathbf c + e^{At}\mathbf c'$, so we need $e^{At}\mathbf c' = \mathbf g$, that is $\mathbf c' = e^{-At}\mathbf g$. Integrating,

$$\mathbf x(t) = e^{At}\mathbf x_0 + \int_0^t e^{A(t-s)}\mathbf g(s)\,ds.$$

Each bit of forcing $\mathbf g(s)\,ds$ applied at time $s$ is carried forward by the homogeneous flow for the remaining time $t - s$, and the effects add up. For example, with $A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ we have $e^{Au} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos u & \sin u\\ -\sin u & \cos u\end{pmatrix}$, and for $\mathbf g = (0, 1)^T$, $\mathbf x_0 = 0$ the formula gives $\mathbf x(t) = \int_0^t(\sin u, \cos u)^T du = (1 - \cos t, \sin t)^T$. This is the system form of $y'' + y = 1$, $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$.

blocks.title: Real distinct eigenvalues
blocks.body: Solve $x' = x + y$, $y' = 4x + y$ with $x(0) = 2$, $y(0) = 0$, and describe what happens as $t \to \infty$.
blocks.solution:
$A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $(1-\lambda)^2 - 4$, so $\lambda = 3$ and $\lambda = -1$. For $\lambda = 3$: $(A - 3I)\mathbf v = 0$ gives $-2v_1 + v_2 = 0$, so $\mathbf v = (1, 2)$. For $\lambda = -1$: $2v_1 + v_2 = 0$, so $\mathbf v = (1, -2)$. Hence

$$\mathbf x(t) = c_1e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix} + c_2e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}.$$

At $t = 0$: $c_1 + c_2 = 2$ and $2c_1 - 2c_2 = 0$, so $c_1 = c_2 = 1$, and $x = e^{3t} + e^{-t}$, $y = 2e^{3t} - 2e^{-t}$.

As $t \to \infty$ the $e^{-t}$ part dies and the solution lines up with the direction $(1, 2)$, growing like $e^{3t}$. Only solutions starting exactly on the line through $(1,-2)$ decay. The origin is a saddle.

blocks.title: Complex eigenvalues: a decaying spiral
blocks.body: Find the general real solution of $x' = -x - 2y$, $y' = 2x - y$.
blocks.solution:
$A = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & -2\\ 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $(\lambda + 1)^2 + 4$, so $\lambda = -1 \pm 2i$. For $\lambda = -1 + 2i$, the first row of $A - \lambda I$ is $(-2i, -2)$, so $\mathbf v = (1, -i) = (1, 0) + i(0, -1)$. Thus $\mathbf a = (1, 0)$ and $\mathbf b = (0, -1)$, and the two real solutions are

$$e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}\cos 2t\\ \sin 2t\end{pmatrix}, \qquad e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}\sin 2t\\ -\cos 2t\end{pmatrix}.$$

The general solution is $c_1$ times the first plus $c_2$ times the second. Every solution circles the origin anticlockwise with angular speed 2 while its distance from the origin shrinks like $e^{-t}$: a stable spiral. One can check this directly: $\frac{d}{dt}(x^2 + y^2) = 2x(-x - 2y) + 2y(2x - y) = -2(x^2 + y^2)$.

blocks.title: A repeated eigenvalue
blocks.body: Compute $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and write down the general solution of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$.
blocks.solution:
The trace is 4 and the determinant is 4, so the characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda - 2)^2$. Put $N = A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & -1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Then $N^2 = 0$, so

$$e^{At} = e^{2t}(I + tN) = e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}1 - t & -t\\ t & 1 + t\end{pmatrix}.$$

Only one eigenvector direction exists: $N\mathbf v = 0$ gives $\mathbf v = (1, -1)$. A generalised eigenvector with $N\mathbf w = \mathbf v$ is $\mathbf w = (-1, 0)$. The general solution is

$$c_1e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} + c_2e^{2t}\left(t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\right),$$

and the columns of $e^{At}$ are the particular choices with $\mathbf x(0) = (1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. The factor $t$ is the signature of a repeated eigenvalue without a full set of eigenvectors.

blocks.title: Three functions chasing each other
blocks.body: Functions $f, g, h$ satisfy $f' = g$, $g' = h$, $h' = f$, with $f(0) = 1$ and $g(0) = h(0) = 0$. Find $f$, and show that $f^3 + g^3 + h^3 - 3fgh = 1$ for all $t$.
blocks.solution:
The matrix of the system is the cyclic shift $A = \begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $A^3 = I$, so its eigenvalues are the cube roots of unity $1, \omega, \omega^2$, where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$. Since $f''' = f$, $f$ is a combination of $e^t$, $e^{\omega t}$, $e^{\omega^2t}$, and the initial data $f(0) = 1$, $f'(0) = g(0) = 0$, $f''(0) = h(0) = 0$ give

$$f(t) = \frac{e^t + e^{\omega t} + e^{\omega^2t}}{3} = \frac{e^t + 2e^{-t/2}\cos\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}t\bigr)}{3}.$$

(Its derivatives at 0 are $\frac13(1 + \omega^k + \omega^{2k})$, which is 1 for $k = 0$ and 0 for $k = 1, 2$.)

For the identity, let $Q = f^3 + g^3 + h^3 - 3fgh$. Differentiating and using the equations,

$$Q' = 3f^2g + 3g^2h + 3h^2f - 3(g\cdot gh + f\cdot hh + fg\cdot f) = 0.$$

So $Q$ is constant, and $Q(0) = 1$. No formula for $f$, $g$, $h$ was needed for this part: finding a conserved quantity is often easier than solving.

blocks.body:
- An eigenvector solution is $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$, not $e^{\lambda t}$ times an arbitrary vector; the vector must be an eigenvector of that $\lambda$.
- With a repeated eigenvalue, $te^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ alone is not a solution; the extra term $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf w$ is essential.
- $e^{A+B} = e^Ae^B$ only when $AB = BA$. In particular, for non-constant $A(t)$, $\exp\int A$ is generally not a solution.
- For complex eigenvalues, the real and imaginary parts of one complex solution already give two independent real solutions; the conjugate eigenvalue adds nothing new.
- The constant equilibrium $-A^{-1}\mathbf b$ needs $A$ invertible; if $0$ is an eigenvalue there may be no equilibrium at all, and a particular solution has to be found another way, for instance by variation of parameters.

For $2\times2$ systems, the signs of the eigenvalues give a picture of all solutions at once, classifying the origin as a saddle, node, spiral or centre; nonlinear systems look like their linearisation near an equilibrium. This is the subject of [[phase-plane]]. The matrix exponential reappears as the solution operator $e^{tQ}$ of continuous-time [[markov-chains]], and as the exponential map from [[lie-algebras]] to [[lie-groups]]. Large stiff systems are solved approximately by the methods of [[numerical-odes]], and separating variables in the [[heat-equation]] produces an infinite version of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ with a diagonal $A$.

1. Solve $x' = 2x + y$, $y' = x + 2y$ with $x(0) = 1$, $y(0) = 3$.
2. Find the normal modes and frequencies of the coupled masses $x_1'' = -2x_1 + x_2$, $x_2'' = x_1 - 2x_2$ by looking for solutions $\cos(\omega t)\mathbf v$.
3. Show that if every eigenvalue of $A$ has negative real part, every solution of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ tends to $0$. (Treat the diagonalisable case first.)
4. Use the Abel–Liouville formula to compute the Wronskian of any two solutions of $\mathbf x' = \begin{pmatrix}1 & t\\ 0 & -3\end{pmatrix}\mathbf x$, up to a constant.
